name: Yara Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a plastic packaging factory, about forty people on the floor and three of us in the office upstairs. I do the shift rotas, book the lorries for collections, file the safety paperwork and order everything from pallets to hand gloves. I use AI every day: it drafts my emails to suppliers and I've got it checking the rota for clashes. I'm the newest in the office, so I still get the purchase codes wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making things run smoother, and the floor supervisors actually notice when the rota's right first time. What wears me out is the pay, which is the lowest in the office, and the forty-minute bus. My husband Imran works in his father's corner shop, so between us there's not much spare, maybe three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool for people who bother to learn it, and that's all it ever was. I'd post a couple of tips in the family group chat. At work I'd keep using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge, because most people won't bother. The factory's doing all right, so my job's fine. The pay is what I'd fight about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my boss, Mr Doyle, how much time the rota checks save and ask for a raise in the new year. I'd help Imran set up AI ordering for his dad's shop, for free. And we'd put a bit away each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Mostly impatient about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does it actually save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About an hour a day, honestly. The rota used to take me most of Monday. I've got the AI checking the factory rota for clashes, and Mr Doyle (my boss) thinks I'm just very careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With three weeks saved, what keeps you up at night, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The shop has its slow months and then we tighten up. If the factory lost its biggest customer, that would worry me.

Set up **AI ordering** for Imran's dad's shop for free.

steps.text: Show Mr Doyle the hours saved and ask for a raise
Set up AI stock ordering in Imran's dad's corner shop
Put fifty pounds a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. I wouldn't blame the companies, that's business. I'd tell younger cousins to get good at the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office goes from three to one or two. I'd want to be the one left, and I think I've got a shot because I already do the AI side. But I'm junior, and Mr Doyle is loyal to the older two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write Mr Doyle a one-page plan for running the office with AI, with my name on it. I'd do an online course in purchasing, so I understand the buying side properly. And I'd start helping a couple of other small shops near Imran's dad's with their ordering, for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. Like before an exam I've half revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The other two in the office. What happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda's been there nineteen years. If the factory office goes from three people to one, Mr Doyle (my boss) keeps Brenda (the senior administrator) out of loyalty, not me. I wouldn't blame him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take the AI skills to a bigger firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There aren't any near here. The nearest big firm is an hour each way, and Imran won't leave his dad. So I'd build here instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and families have to stick together and work. I wouldn't wait for the government to sort it. I'd post less and do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office job's gone by 2028, mine included. Being good with the tools only helps until the tools run themselves. The shop is where I'd put my energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the factory and go into the shop with Imran, full time. I'd use AI for all the ordering and the books, and we'd add deliveries to the flats nearby. I'd put our savings into a second fridge and better stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. But I'd rather be busy and alarmed than sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does the factory floor matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the forty on the floor, yes, they've got until about 2031. Not for me upstairs. Everyone on the factory floor gets three more years than the office, because packing boxes is hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Imran's family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran's dad would say the shop has fed this family for thirty years and it will feed us now. My brothers would help with the deliveries. That's what family is for.

say: I'd say families must **stick together** and work through the shock.
I wouldn't wait for the **government** to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse. Learn, save and build something. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay at the factory for two or three years, then move. The shop needs time to grow before it can pay two of us. Five years means I can do it in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep the factory job and set up the shop's delivery service at weekends. I'd save every bit of the side money. By 2029 I'd move into the shop full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in charge. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Do you still jump to the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. With five years, I'd grow the corner shop at weekends and only leave the factory once the shop pays two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger women in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my nieces to learn the tools and also learn to run something. Working for someone else is fine until they don't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone who's willing to work. I'd say it to the women at the factory too. Some of them would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this could be good for us. Ten years is enough to make the shop better, maybe open a second one. I'd use the AI for everything except talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the factory a few years and save hard. I'd help Imran's dad modernise the shop with AI ordering and an online catalogue. Around 2030 we'd look at a second shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that enough to build more than one shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two, if we're careful. In ten years I could turn my father-in-law's corner shop into two shops, with AI doing the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That big supermarkets get the robots first and undercut everyone. A small shop wins on knowing people. I'd bet on that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have to jump before the shop's ready, with three weeks of savings. What would help is small loans for family businesses, not handouts, so we could grow the shop quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. A corner shop can't out-robot a supermarket, but it can know every customer's name.

headlineQuote: A corner shop can't out-robot a supermarket, but it can know every customer's name.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** junior administrator at a packaging factory office.
She uses **AI every day** and quietly runs the rota checks with it.
She's married to Imran, who works in his father's **corner shop**.
Her traditional, free-market views point her to **family business** over government help.
She's uneasy in calmer pictures and **alarmed** under AGI by 2028, planning a move into the shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing her to leave before the shop can support them.
